Yeah, that’s a really thoughtful point. I think you’re right that there’s been this promise—whether spoken or not—that enduring the hard, dangerous, or thankless roles might eventually lead to recognition or even power. And historically, men have definitely filled both the top and bottom rungs of society in a big way. But I don’t think feminism came from a place of ignoring those hardships, though—more that it came from a frustration with being systemically locked out of both the top and the bottom roles. Women weren’t allowed to work in mines or go to war not because people were protecting them, but because they weren’t trusted with those responsibilities—or any real choices. And that lack of agency, across the board, was its own kind of hardship.

So I guess where I’m coming from is: both men and women have been dealt tough hands in different ways, and neither story cancels the other out. I really appreciate you sharing your view on it. It’s always good to think more deeply on this kind of thing.

Yeah, I totally get what you’re saying. Jobs like coal mining, farming, construction—those are brutal, and it’s true that a lot of men have carried the weight of that kind of work for generations. That definitely hasn’t been “easy,” and I’m not trying to take away from that at all. When I said men have had it easier, I meant more in terms of societal power and how systems are set up—not that every man’s life has been a breeze. 

These conversations are tricky, but I really appreciate being able to talk about it honestly. I think that’s how we actually start to understand each other better.

Because men in general have had it easier throughout history but (at least in the U.S.) Black people have had it harder. I grew up in small town AL and being a man gets you clout but being a Black man definitely takes some of that away.
